top5.diagnosis: Parasitic Infection (e.g., Strongyloides stercoralis or Toxocara)
top5.rationale: Must be rigorously excluded as a primary cause of eosinophilia and GI inflammation before diagnosing idiopathic EGE, despite negative initial stool studies.
Considered if eosinophilia persists without an identifiable secondary cause like allergy or parasites, though the localized mucosal findings favor EGE.
Can mimic EGE with pancreatic/biliary enzyme elevation and tissue eosinophilia, but normal serum IgG4 makes this less likely than EGE.

top5.diagnosis: Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS) or Drug-Induced Eosinophilia
top5.rationale: Although medication review was negative, occult drug reactions can present with visceral eosinophilia and require re-evaluation of all supplements/OTC meds.

Histologic confirmation of eosinophilic infiltration across multiple GI sites combined with peripheral eosinophilia and markedly elevated lipase suggests EGE causing pancreatic duct obstruction or direct inflammation.
Persistent absolute eosinophilia >1500/µL for weeks with end-organ damage (GI tract, pancreas) and exclusion of secondary causes like parasites or drugs fits the diagnostic criteria for HES.

The strikingly high lipase levels in the context of normal pancreatic imaging on CT may indicate a rare variant where eosinophils infiltrate the pancreas directly, often associated with underlying atopic disease or EG.
Although stool O&P was negative, single-sample sensitivity is low; this must remain a top differential due to the risk of hyperinfection syndrome if steroids are administered without prior screening.

While serum IgG4 is normal, tissue diagnosis can still be positive in up to 30% of cases, and it mimics both pancreatitis and eosinophilic disorders, though the prominent peripheral eosinophilia makes this less likely than EGE.
Unifying diagnosis explaining panhypopituitarism (central AI, hypoT4, DI), stalk thickening, and mass effect in a young female with autoimmune background.
Classic sellar-suprasellar mass with necrosis/calcification causing DI and anterior pituitary deficits, though less likely to present with such rapid progressive asthenia without visual crisis.
Midline tumor common in adolescents causing DI and hypopituitarism; must be ruled out despite normal CSF markers as they can be negative early or in non-secreting variants.

Explains mass effect and hormonal deficits, but central DI is rare in adenomas unless there is significant suprasellar extension or prior surgery/radiation, making this less likely than inflammatory causes.
Can cause stalk thickening, panhypopituitarism, and DI, but typically presents with systemic signs or abnormal chest imaging/CSF findings which are absent here.
Peripheral eosinophilia combined with diffuse GI mucosal eosinophilic infiltration and chronic symptoms in a diabetic patient fits the classic presentation.
Geographic/travel history is denied but must be rigorously excluded as a primary cause of eosinophilia and GI symptoms before diagnosing idiopathic conditions.
Persistent absolute eosinophilia >1500/µL with end-organ damage (GI tract) requires exclusion of clonal or reactive HES despite normal smear morphology.
Although serum IgG4 is normal, tissue diagnosis can still yield IgG4-RD; however, the prominent eosinophilia makes this less likely than EGE.

top5.diagnosis: Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS)
top5.rationale: Medication review was negative, but occult exposure to supplements or herbal remedies common in patients with metabolic comorbidities remains a differential.
Classic triad of diabetes insipidus, pituitary stalk thickening, and lytic sellar/suprasellar mass in a child/adolescent; CD1a/Langerin positivity is the hallmark histologic clue.
Most common malignant germ cell tumor causing panhypopituitarism and DI in adolescents; PLAP/c-kit positive on biopsy, often associated with elevated beta-hCG or AFP if mixed.

Solid-cystic suprasellar mass causing hypopituitarism and visual defects; though typically calcified on CT, non-calcified solid variants occur, and adamantinomatous type shows wet keratin/beta-catenin mutations.
Rare in children but must be considered given rapid onset of multiple anterior/posterior pituitary deficits; requires identification of primary source via immunohistochemistry.

Associated with other autoimmune conditions (T1DM, Hashimoto's); presents with stalk thickening and mass effect, but central necrosis and significant DI are less typical than in neoplastic/infiltrative causes.
Classic triad of diabetes insipidus, pituitary stalk thickening, and lytic sellar mass in an adolescent with autoimmune comorbidities.
Most common malignant sellar-suprasellar tumor in adolescents causing panhypopituitarism and DI; often presents with stalk thickening and necrosis.
Common suprasellar mass in this age group causing visual defects and hypopituitarism, though pure solid/necrotic presentation without calcification is less typical.
Autoimmune thyroiditis suggests susceptibility to inflammatory conditions; necrotic mass with stalk thickening can mimic tumors but requires infectious/inflammatory exclusion.
Rare in 14-year-olds but must be considered given rapid progression, weight loss, and necrotic mass; history of appendectomy is likely incidental.
Classic triad of central adrenal insufficiency, central hypothyroidism, and diabetes insipidus with stalk thickening in a young female strongly favors autoimmune inflammation over neoplasm.
Sellar-suprasellar mass with necrosis and calcification potential fits the imaging, though DI is less common as an initial presentation compared to hypophysitis.
Must be ruled out in any adolescent with suprasellar mass and DI; normal CSF cytology does not exclude it, requiring tumor markers (AFP/bHCG) for definitive exclusion.
Explains mass effect and hormonal deficits, but the prominent diabetes insipidus and stalk thickening are atypical for pure adenomas without significant invasion.

top5.diagnosis: Granulomatous Disease (e.g., Sarcoidosis or Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis)
top5.rationale: Systemic granulomatous infiltration can mimic this exact radiologic and endocrine profile, though lack of other systemic signs makes it less likely than primary pituitary pathology.
The gold standard for diagnosis is histologic confirmation of eosinophilic infiltration in the GI tract with exclusion of other causes; this case fits perfectly despite the atypical pancreatitis.

top5.diagnosis: Parasitic Infection (e.g., Strongyloides stercoralis or Toxocara)
top5.rationale: A critical mimic that must be ruled out before diagnosing EGE; negative stool O&P has low sensitivity for tissue-invasive parasites like Strongyloides, which can cause both eosinophilia and GI symptoms.

While peripheral eosinophils are elevated, HES requires organ damage attributable to eosinophils; however, the lack of cardiac/pulmonary findings and normal IgG4 makes primary EGE more likely than systemic HES.

top5.diagnosis: Drug-Induced Acute Pancreatitis with secondary eosinophilia
top5.rationale: The striking lipase elevation suggests pancreatic injury; while meds were 'reviewed,' subtle drug reactions (e.g., ACE inhibitors for HTN) can cause both pancreatitis and eosinophilia, though diffuse mucosal biopsy changes argue against this as the sole cause.
Can present with autoimmune pancreatitis and eosinophilia, but the normal serum IgG4 level and lack of storiform fibrosis/obliterative phlebitis on biopsy make this highly unlikely compared to EGE.

Strongest alternative to neoplasm; explains panhypopituitarism, stalk thickening, and hyperprolactinemia in a young female with existing autoimmune diathesis (T1DM, thyroiditis) without requiring a mass effect large enough to cause necrosis.

Classic 'great mimicker' in this demographic; central DI is often the earliest sign preceding visible mass, and it fits the suprasellar location, but the solid/necrotic description and lack of hemorrhage make it less typical than cystic variants.

Most common sellar-suprasellar tumor in children/adolescents causing these symptoms, but typically presents with calcifications or cystic components rather than a purely solid enhancing mass with central necrosis.

Explains mass effect and hypopituitarism, but rarely causes diabetes insipidus unless very large/invasive, and the rapid onset of multiple hormonal deficits plus necrosis is atypical for benign adenomas.

top5.diagnosis: Granulomatous Disease (e.g., Sarcoidosis or Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis)
top5.rationale: Can cause stalk thickening and DI, but normal chest radiography, unremarkable abdominal ultrasound, and normal inflammatory markers significantly lower the probability compared to isolated pituitary pathology.
The definitive diagnosis supported by CD117/tryptase positivity, metachromatic granules, and clinical presentation of a solitary plaque, despite the atypical histologic progression.

Must be ruled out due to the alarming increase in mitotic activity (9/mm2), high Ki-67 index (29.5%), and nuclear pleomorphism on excision, which are hallmarks of malignancy rather than benign mastocytoma.

A critical differential given the patient's history of melanoma and MiTF positivity; however, the specific mast cell markers (tryptase, CD117) and lack of epidermal involvement make this less likely than primary mast cell disease.
Unlikely due to normal serum tryptase, absence of systemic symptoms, and no evidence of systemic disease on imaging, but remains a consideration if bone marrow biopsy were performed.
Considered due to spindle cells and pleomorphism, but definitively excluded by the strong immunophenotypic profile for mast cells (CD117+, Tryptase+).
Solitary plaque with CD117+/tryptase+ mast cells and normal serum tryptase fits the classic presentation of a solitary cutaneous mastocytoma.

The rapid progression to high mitotic rate (9/mm2), elevated Ki-67 (29.5%), and significant nuclear pleomorphism upon excision raises concern for malignant transformation or primary sarcomatous behavior despite initial benign appearance.

History of melanoma and MiTF positivity are red flags; however, strong CD117/tryptase expression and Giemsa-positive granules make this less likely than mast cell lineage, though dedifferentiated metastasis remains a critical differential.
Normal serum tryptase and lack of systemic symptoms/imaging findings argue strongly against this, but it must be ruled out given the neoplastic nature of the lesion.
A common yellowish plaque on the temple in a middle-aged man is often BCC, but the immunoprofile (CD117+, tryptase+) and histology (epithelioid sheets) definitively exclude this diagnosis.
Diagnosis of exclusion supported by normal structural exams, negative biopsies, and inconclusive VFSS due to behavioral avoidance rather than mechanical obstruction.
Classic presentation in adolescents with solid-food dysphagia; however, ruled out here by normal endoscopic biopsies, making it a critical differential that was appropriately excluded.

top5.diagnosis: Esophageal Motility Disorder (e.g., Achalasia or DES)
top5.rationale: Can present with intermittent dysphagia and globus sensation; less likely given normal barium swallow and lack of regurgitation/weight loss, but manometry would be the definitive test.
Psychiatric history of self-harm/anxiety combined with inconsistent objective findings (normal ENT/barium) and disproportionate functional impairment suggests a psychogenic mechanism.
Rare cause of dysphagia/vomiting in thin adolescents; unlikely without weight loss or postprandial pain, but considered in organic differentials for young females with feeding difficulties.
Solitary plaque with metachromatic granules and CD117/tryptase positivity fits the classic presentation of a solitary mast cell tumor in an adult.

The rapid progression to high mitotic activity (9/mm2), elevated Ki-67 (29.5%), and nuclear pleomorphism upon excision suggests malignant transformation or initial misclassification of a low-grade sarcoma.
History of melanoma combined with MiTF positivity and epithelioid morphology creates a diagnostic overlap; however, tryptase/Giemsa positivity strongly favors mast cell lineage over melanocytic.

Although serum tryptase is normal and no systemic disease was found on imaging, the presence of CD25+ cells and KIT wild-type status requires exclusion of indolent systemic involvement despite the solitary lesion appearance.

A rare mimic that can present as a yellowish plaque with epithelioid cells; while CD117 is typically negative, aberrant expression or diagnostic confusion with mast cell markers necessitates consideration in aggressive vascular tumors.
Solitary plaque with CD117+/tryptase+ epithelioid mast cells and metachromatic granules fits the classic presentation, despite atypical high-grade features.
The excision specimen's high mitotic rate (9/mm²), Ki-67 index (29.5%), and nuclear pleomorphism meet WHO criteria for sarcomatous transformation of a solitary mast cell tumor.
History of melanoma plus MiTF positivity creates a diagnostic pitfall; however, strong tryptase/CD117 positivity and Giemsa granules favor mast cell lineage over melanocytic.
Absence of KIT mutations (exons 8-17) is unusual for systemic disease but can occur in localized cutaneous forms, requiring exclusion of other myeloid neoplasms.
Epithelioid morphology and CD30 heterogeneity might suggest vascular tumors, but specific mast cell markers (tryptase, CD117) and metachromasia rule this out.
Diagnosis of exclusion supported by normal structural workup (endoscopy, barium swallow), normal labs, and psychogenic features like globus sensation and anxiety.
High pre-test probability in a young patient with solid food dysphagia; must be ruled out definitively despite 'normal' biopsies if sampling was inadequate or patchy.

top5.diagnosis: Esophageal Motility Disorder (e.g., Achalasia or Distal Esophageal Spasm)
top5.rationale: Barium swallow can be normal in early achalasia; requires manometry to exclude neuromuscular dysfunction not seen on endoscopy.
Strong association with history of self-harm/anxiety and the specific finding of prolonged water swallowing time suggesting voluntary inhibition or functional motor control issues.
Rare but possible cause of intermittent obstruction/dysphagia-like symptoms in adolescents; often missed without specific CT angiography focus.
Normal barium swallow, endoscopy, and labs combined with prolonged water swallow time and anxiety history strongly support a functional etiology over organic obstruction.
Classic presentation of solid food dysphagia in an adolescent; however, normal biopsies make this unlikely unless sampling error occurred or the disease is patchy and missed.

top5.diagnosis: Esophageal Motility Disorder (e.g., Achalasia or Diffuse Esophageal Spasm)
top5.rationale: Barium swallow can be normal in early achalasia; VFSS was inconclusive due to poor cooperation, leaving manometry as the necessary next step to rule out neuromuscular dysfunction.
History of self-harm and anxiety, coupled with inconsistent objective findings (normal exams vs. severe subjective limitation) and refusal of invasive testing, suggests a psychogenic overlay.
Although weight loss is denied, subtle anatomical compression could cause intermittent symptoms; however, normal abdominal exam and lack of vomiting make this a low-probability outlier.

top5.diagnosis: Cutaneous Mastocytoma with KIT Wild-Type Status
top5.rationale: The leading hypothesis fits the histology (CD117+/Tryptase+) and clinical presentation, but the absence of KIT mutations is atypical for adult solitary mastocytomas, which usually harbor D816V; this discrepancy suggests a non-clonal or reactive process rather than classic neoplastic mastocytosis.

The rapid progression to high mitotic activity (9/mm2), significant nuclear pleomorphism, and Ki-67 index of 29.5% upon excision contradicts the benign nature of a mastocytoma and aligns better with the aggressive behavior of sarcoma, despite the initial low-grade biopsy.

Given the history of melanoma, epithelioid cells with MiTF positivity could represent metastatic disease; however, strong CD117/Tryptase positivity makes this unlikely unless there is aberrant expression or collision tumor, but it remains a critical alternative to rule out due to patient history.

top5.diagnosis: Reactive Mast Cell Hyperplasia secondary to underlying malignancy
top5.rationale: Solitary plaques with wild-type KIT and normal tryptase may represent a paraneoplastic or reactive accumulation of mast cells driven by cytokines from an occult systemic process or local irritation, explaining the lack of clonal mutation.

Epithelioid morphology and granular cytoplasm can mimic vascular tumors; while CD117 is typically negative in endothelial cells, some variants show aberrant marker expression, and the 'yellowish' plaque appearance might suggest lipid-laden macrophages or xanthomatous change associated with vascular anomalies.
Normal structural workup (endoscopy, barium, labs) combined with significant anxiety history and psychosocial stressors points to a functional disorder.
Classic demographic (adolescent) and presentation (solid food dysphagia, choking episodes) warrant re-evaluation of biopsies for eosinophilia despite initial 'normal' report.

top5.diagnosis: Esophageal Motility Disorder (e.g., Achalasia or Distal Esophageal Spasm)
top5.rationale: Prolonged water swallow time and solid-food restriction suggest neuromuscular dysfunction not captured by static imaging or standard endoscopy.
History of self-harm and untreated psychiatric comorbidities increases risk for somatic symptom disorders manifesting as dysphagia without organic cause.
Potential use of SSRIs or other psychotropics for prior depression/anxiety could contribute to motility issues or subtle mucosal irritation missed on gross exam.
Strong temporal association with herbal medicine initiation in an elderly patient with CKD, presenting with classic ILD markers (elevated KL-6/SP-D) and exclusion of other causes.
Fourfold rise in complement fixation titers confirms recent infection, which can trigger severe pneumonitis or diffuse alveolar damage mimicking drug toxicity.

top5.diagnosis: Diffuse Alveolar Hemorrhage secondary to Drug-Induced Lung Injury
top5.rationale: BAL findings of hemorrhage with neutrophil predominance are a known, albeit less common, severe manifestation of herbal medicine-induced pneumonitis.

top5.diagnosis: Acute Exacerbation of Undiagnosed Interstitial Lung Disease
top5.rationale: Age and smoking history are risk factors for subclinical ILD; Sai-rei-to may have acted as the precipitating insult for an acute exacerbation.

top5.diagnosis: Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction (HFpEF) with Pulmonary Edema
top5.rationale: Hypertension, CKD, elevated BNP, and pleural effusions suggest cardiac contribution, though normal EF and lack of response to diuretics alone make it less likely than inflammatory causes.
High-dose methylprednisolone and tapering prednisone precipitated severe hyperglycemia (1240 mg/dL) and ketosis in a patient with prior pancreatic injury.

top5.diagnosis: SLE-associated pancreatitis leading to secondary diabetes mellitus
top5.rationale: History of idiopathic pancreatitis ages 12-16 suggests underlying exocrine/endocrine damage, creating a substrate for rapid beta-cell failure under steroid stress.

top5.diagnosis: Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 3b (SLE and Type 1 Diabetes)
top5.rationale: The coexistence of SLE and abrupt-onset DKA raises suspicion for concurrent autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta-cells, independent of steroid effects.
Recent cyclophosphamide boluses may have caused subclinical pancreatic inflammation or direct islet cell toxicity, exacerbating glucose intolerance.
While labs confirm DKA, the initial drowsiness and seizures could be compounded by active CNS lupus, requiring differentiation from pure metabolic causes.

top5.diagnosis: New-onset Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus presenting as Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
top5.rationale: High-dose cyclophosphamide and steroids in a young woman with prior idiopathic pancreatitis suggest autoimmune beta-cell destruction unmasked by immunosuppression.
Recent pulse methylprednisolone and high-dose prednisone taper directly precipitated severe hyperglycemia and ketosis in a susceptible host.
The coexistence of SLE and new-onset insulin-dependent diabetes fits the clustering of autoimmune endocrinopathies common in Mestizo populations.

top5.diagnosis: Cyclophosphamide-Associated Pancreatic Toxicity leading to Insulin Deficiency
top5.rationale: History of 'idiopathic' pancreatitis may represent early autoimmune or drug-induced pancreatic injury, now culminating in absolute insulin deficiency.

top5.diagnosis: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS) overlapping with DKA
top5.rationale: Extreme glucose (1240 mg/dL) and osmolarity (322.8 mOsm/kg) indicate a mixed picture driven by profound dehydration and osmotic diuresis from steroid use.

top5.diagnosis: Cyclophosphamide-induced acute pancreatitis leading to new-onset Type 3c diabetes mellitus and diabetic ketoacidosis
top5.rationale: Temporal link between cyclophosphamide dose and DKA; history of idiopathic pancreatitis suggests underlying pancreatic vulnerability or prior subclinical damage unmasked by drug toxicity.

top5.diagnosis: Steroid-induced hyperglycemia precipitating DKA in undiagnosed latent autoimmune diabetes (LADA)
top5.rationale: High-dose methylprednisolone/prednisone causes insulin resistance; LADA is common in SLE patients and may present as DKA under metabolic stress despite normal BMI.

top5.diagnosis: SLE-associated autoimmune pancreatitis causing exocrine-endocrine failure
top5.rationale: Rare but documented complication where lupus vasculitis or immune complex deposition damages pancreatic tissue, leading to insulin deficiency and subsequent DKA.

top5.diagnosis: Phenytoin-induced inhibition of insulin secretion contributing to severe hyperglycemia
top5.rationale: Phenytoin blocks voltage-gated calcium channels in beta cells, reducing insulin release; combined with steroids, this can tip a compensated patient into frank DKA.

top5.diagnosis: Concurrent viral myocarditis/pancreatitis (e.g., Coxsackievirus) mimicking SLE flare complications
top5.rationale: Viral infections are common triggers for both SLE flares and acute pancreatitis/DKA; the 'idiopathic' past episodes might have been unrecognized viral etiologies now recurring.

top5.diagnosis: Steroid-induced diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) in the setting of underlying Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
top5.rationale: High-dose methylprednisolone and prednisone precipitated severe hyperglycemia and ketosis; the history of 'idiopathic pancreatitis' likely represents prior episodes of undiagnosed DKA misinterpreted as abdominal pain.

top5.diagnosis: New-onset Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus unmasked by corticosteroid therapy
top5.rationale: The patient's age, autoimmune background (SLE), and previous 'pancreatitis' episodes suggest latent autoimmune diabetes that was clinically silent until steroid-induced insulin resistance overwhelmed beta-cell reserve.

top5.diagnosis: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus with secondary Sjögren's syndrome causing exocrine pancreatic insufficiency
top5.rationale: While less likely to cause frank DKA without absolute insulin deficiency, autoimmune destruction of pancreatic tissue could explain both the past 'pancreatitis' and current metabolic decompensation if endocrine function was compromised.

top5.diagnosis: Cyclophosphamide-induced acute pancreatitis leading to transient insulinopenia
top5.rationale: Although amylase/lipase are normal now, cyclophosphamide is a known cause of pancreatitis; however, this is a weaker fit for the profound DKA compared to steroid effects, making it a differential rather than primary cause.

top5.diagnosis: Neuropsychiatric SLE with concurrent organic brain syndrome due to severe metabolic derangement
top5.rationale: The drowsiness and seizures may be exacerbated or mimicked by the extreme hyperosmolarity and acidosis, representing a combined diagnosis where the psychiatric/neurologic presentation is driven by the metabolic crisis.
Endemic origin, madarosis, and nodular lesions unresponsive to penicillin suggest mycobacterial infection; RPR reactivity is a known biological false positive in leprosy.

top5.diagnosis: Secondary Syphilis with Treatment Failure or Reinfection
top5.rationale: High initial RPR titer and reactive treponemal test confirm syphilis, but persistent lesions despite adequate therapy require exclusion of neurosyphilis, HIV co-infection (though ELISA negative), or non-adherence.
Can mimic syphilitic nodules and cause hair loss; however, the specific combination of madarosis and endemic exposure makes infectious etiologies more probable first.
Chronic granulomatous skin lesions in an endemic region can present as nodules/ulcers; requires histologic confirmation via acid-fast bacilli staining and culture.

top5.diagnosis: Deep Fungal Infection (e.g., Chromoblastomycosis or Sporotrichosis)
top5.rationale: Chronic ulcerative nodules on extremities are characteristic; less likely given the systemic symptoms like madarosis and fatigue, but remains a differential for treatment-resistant cutaneous nodules.
The triad of madarosis, xerosis, and nodular lesions in an endemic region is pathognomonic; the low RPR titer represents a biological false positive common in leprosy, explaining treatment failure.
Initially suspected due to reactive treponemal tests, but ruled out by the lack of clinical response to adequate penicillin therapy and the disproportionately low RPR titer for active disease.
Endemic in Colombia and presents with ulcerated nodules, but typically lacks the systemic signs of madarosis and diffuse xerosis seen in this case.
Can present with red-brown papulonodular lesions and fatigue, but the specific combination of eyebrow loss and high-titer biological false-positive serology strongly favors infectious etiology.
A differential for chronic nodular skin lesions, but less likely given the bilateral symmetric distribution on ankles/forearms and absence of aquatic exposure history.

High-dose methylprednisolone and prednisone taper are potent diabetogenic agents that precipitate DKA in susceptible individuals, explaining the acute hyperglycemia and acidosis without requiring a new autoimmune etiology.

top5.diagnosis: Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 3 (SLE + Type 1 Diabetes)
top5.rationale: The history of idiopathic pancreatitis suggests prior subclinical beta-cell destruction or autoimmune pancreatic involvement, making concurrent SLE and latent T1DM unmasked by stress/steroids a plausible unified diagnosis.

top5.diagnosis: Cyclophosphamide-induced pancreatic toxicity leading to insulin deficiency
top5.rationale: Although amylase/lipase are normal now, cyclophosphamide can cause direct acinar/beta-cell injury; the temporal link to the sixth dose supports drug-induced secondary diabetes rather than primary autoimmune onset.

top5.diagnosis: Neuropsychiatric SLE with hypothalamic-pituitary axis disruption
top5.rationale: NPSLE involving the hypothalamus could dysregulate glucose metabolism and counter-regulatory hormones, though this rarely causes such profound DKA without underlying beta-cell failure.

top5.diagnosis: Concurrent viral myocarditis or sepsis triggering metabolic decompensation
top5.rationale: Tachycardia and tachypnea may indicate an occult infectious trigger (e.g., CMV, HSV) common in immunosuppressed patients, which precipitated DKA in a patient with borderline glucose tolerance.

Classic triad of nodular skin lesions, madarosis (eyebrow loss), and xerosis in an endemic region; the low RPR titer with reactive treponemal test represents a biological false positive common in leprosy due to cross-reacting antibodies.

Initially suspected due to reactive RPR and nodules, but ruled out by the failure of penicillin therapy, lack of clinical improvement, and discordant serology (high initial RPR vs. low confirmatory RPR).
Endemic in Colombia and presents with ulcerated nodules, but typically lacks systemic signs like madarosis or diffuse xerosis, and does not explain the specific serological paradox.
Can present with red-brown papules/nodules and fatigue, but cutaneous sarcoidosis rarely causes madarosis or significant scaling/ulceration, and does not account for the syphilis serology findings.
Causes nodular/ulcerative skin lesions on extremities, but is usually localized, lacks systemic symptoms like hair loss/fatigue, and has no association with false-positive syphilis tests.
Histologic confirmation of eosinophilic infiltration across multiple GI sites with peripheral eosinophilia and exclusion of secondary causes fits the classic mucosal subtype presentation.
Persistent marked eosinophilia (>1500/µL) with end-organ damage (GI tract) requires ruling out systemic HES, though isolated GI involvement makes primary EG more likely.
A critical mimic that must be definitively excluded via serology or specialized stool exams despite negative initial O&P, as it drives identical histologic findings.
Can cause pancreatic inflammation and GI wall thickening mimicking this case, but normal serum IgG4 and lack of storiform fibrosis make this less likely than EG.
Although medication review was negative, occult exposure to supplements or herbal remedies can trigger eosinophilic tissue infiltration and pancreatitis-like enzyme elevation.
The watershed distribution of white matter lesions in a young woman with recurrent TIA-like symptoms is the hallmark presentation of Moyamoya, often misdiagnosed as MS or psychogenic illness.

top5.diagnosis: Primary Angiitis of the Central Nervous System (PACNS)
top5.rationale: Vasculitis can cause multifocal ischemic changes and enhancement; however, normal CSF and lack of systemic markers make this less likely than structural vasculopathy like Moyamoya.
Initial consideration due to age, sex, and white matter lesions, but the specific watershed distribution and lack of typical periventricular 'Dawson's fingers' or oligoclonal bands argue against it.
A genetic small vessel disease causing white matter hyperintensities and strokes, but typically involves anterior temporal poles and external capsule, not strictly ACA/MCA watershed zones.
Considered due to prior psychiatric attribution, but the objective MRI findings of structural white matter damage definitively rule out a purely functional etiology for the current presentation.

Endemic origin in Colombia, eyebrow loss (madarosis), xerosis, and nodular lesions unresponsive to syphilis treatment are classic for lepromatous leprosy, which often presents with false-positive or low-titer RPR due to cross-reactive antibodies.

High initial RPR titer (1:128) and reactive treponemal test strongly support this, but the lack of clinical response and persistent low titer suggest either a Jarisch-Herxheimer-like non-response, reinfection, or an alternative diagnosis mimicking syphilis serologically.

Geographic exposure in Cali (endemic area) can cause chronic ulcerative/nodular skin lesions; while typically not associated with madarosis or high RPR titers, it is a key differential for non-healing ulcers in this demographic.

Can present with red-brown papules/nodules and systemic symptoms like fatigue; however, it does not explain the specific finding of madarosis or the significant syphilitic serology, making it less likely than leprosy.

Chronic granulomatous skin infection from water exposure (common in coastal/river regions like Cali) causing nodules/ulcers, though it lacks the systemic features (madarosis, xerosis) and serological confounders seen here.

Watershed distribution of white matter lesions with cortical enhancement and no restricted diffusion is the hallmark pathophysiologic signature of chronic hemodynamic failure due to progressive stenosis of the terminal internal carotid arteries.

Large artery atherosclerosis causing flow-limiting stenosis produces identical watershed ischemic injury patterns; must be distinguished from Moyamoya by vessel wall imaging or angiography showing plaque rather than smooth tapering.

top5.diagnosis: Primary Angiitis of the Central Nervous System (PACNS)
top5.rationale: Small-to-medium vessel vasculitis can cause multifocal white matter lesions and enhancement mimicking demyelination, but the specific watershed predominance suggests large-vessel involvement or hypoperfusion secondary to inflammatory stenosis.
If there is an undisclosed history of cranial irradiation, this causes progressive large-vessel stenosis leading to watershed infarcts and white matter changes that mimic Moyamoya syndrome.

Included as a differential for periventricular/subcortical lesions in a young woman, though the strict watershed distribution and lack of CSF oligoclonal bands make primary demyelinating pathology mechanistically unlikely compared to vascular etiologies.

Watershed distribution of white matter lesions in a young woman with recurrent TIA-like symptoms and no inflammatory markers is the classic radiologic signature for this progressive steno-occlusive vasculopathy.

top5.diagnosis: Primary Angiitis of the Central Nervous System (PACNS)
top5.rationale: Can present with multifocal ischemic changes and cortical enhancement; however, the strict watershed pattern and normal CSF make large-vessel or Moyamoya variants more likely than small-vessel PACNS.

Initial consideration due to age, sex, and periventricular/subcortical lesions, but the specific watershed distribution, lack of oligoclonal bands/CSF inflammation, and linear cortical enhancement argue strongly against demyelination.
A common cause of watershed infarcts, though less likely as the primary diagnosis in a 44-year-old with no stated vascular risk factors compared to Moyamoya or vasculitis.

Considered due to subcortical white matter hyperintensities and transient neurological deficits, but typically involves anterior temporal poles and external capsules rather than a pure ACA/MCA watershed distribution.
Explains watershed infarcts and T2/FLAIR lesions in a young woman with no vascular risk factors; often misdiagnosed as MS or psychosomatic issues.

top5.diagnosis: Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL)
top5.rationale: Classic mimic of MS with subcortical white matter changes and recurrent focal deficits, though typically involves anterior temporal poles which may be subtle.

top5.diagnosis: Primary Angiitis of the Central Nervous System (PACNS)
top5.rationale: Can present with multifocal ischemic lesions and enhancement; normal systemic inflammatory markers and CSF do not rule it out due to low sensitivity.
The leading hypothesis, but challenged by the specific watershed distribution of lesions and lack of typical oligoclonal bands or IgG index in CSF.
Triad of encephalopathy, branch retinal artery occlusions, and hearing loss can be incomplete; causes small vessel ischemia that mimics demyelination on MRI.
The watershed distribution of lesions in a young woman with no vascular risk factors is the hallmark radiographic signature of this progressive steno-occlusive arteriopathy.

top5.diagnosis: Primary Angiitis of the Central Nervous System (PACNS)
top5.rationale: Although CSF was unremarkable, PACNS can present with normal inflammatory markers and multifocal ischemic changes mimicking demyelination or watershed infarcts.

top5.diagnosis: Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL)
top5.rationale: A key demographic consideration for recurrent transient neurological deficits and white matter lesions in a middle-aged adult without traditional vascular risk factors.

Despite the atypical watershed distribution, the initial presentation of periventricular/subcortical lesions and cortical enhancement strongly mimics MS, which must remain on the differential until vascular causes are excluded.

Considered due to the combination of encephalopathic features (white matter lesions) and potential microvascular occlusion, though the absence of reported hearing loss or visual symptoms makes it less likely than Moyamoya.

Explains the triad of nodules, eyebrow loss (madarosis), and fatigue; false-positive RPR is a classic serological artifact in lepromatous leprosy due to anticardiolipin antibodies, and lesions persist despite penicillin.

top5.diagnosis: Secondary Syphilis with Jarisch-Herxheimer-like Persistence or Neurosyphilis
top5.rationale: While treatment failure suggests resistance or reinfection, the initial high titer drop to 1:2 indicates response; however, persistent nodules could represent gummatous syphilis requiring longer therapy or neurosyphilis not covered by IM benzathine alone.

top5.diagnosis: Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphoma (Mycosis Fungoides) with incidental latent syphilis
top5.rationale: Chronic pruritic plaques/nodules unresponsive to antibiotics are hallmark CTCL; the reactive treponemal test may reflect past treated infection (serofast state), while the low RPR does not correlate with active disease burden.

top5.diagnosis: Deep Fungal Infection (e.g., Sporotrichosis or Chromoblastomycosis)
top5.rationale: Endemic in Colombia, presents with chronic nodular/ulcerative skin lesions that do not respond to antibacterial therapy; requires specific antifungal treatment which was not administered.
Can present with red-brown papules/nodules and systemic symptoms like fatigue; often misdiagnosed as infectious granulomas and will not resolve with penicillin.

top5.diagnosis: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) with Arterial and Venous Thrombosis
top5.rationale: Classic presentation: thrombocytopenia and multi-territory arterial/venous clots 5-14 days post-heparin exposure, confirmed by citrate tube to rule out pseudothrombocytopenia.
Major mimic of HIT causing arterial strokes and venous thromboembolism; must be ruled out as it can coexist or present similarly, though the temporal link to heparin favors HIT first.

top5.diagnosis: Paradoxical Embolism via Patent Foramen Ovale (PFO)
top5.rationale: Explains simultaneous venous (PE, DVT) and arterial (stroke) events in a patient with normal cardiac structure on echo, though PFO closure is often missed on standard TTE without bubble study.
Unifying diagnosis for hypercoagulability, migratory thrombophlebitis, and constitutional symptoms (fever), though the specific timing relative to heparin makes HIT more probable.
Can cause thrombocytopenia and widespread micro/macrovascular thrombosis, but typically presents with bleeding diathesis and prolonged PT/aPTT, which are not highlighted here.

top5.diagnosis: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) with Arterial and Venous Thrombosis
top5.rationale: Classic timing (day 15 post-exposure), severe thrombocytopenia, and simultaneous arterial stroke and venous PE/hepatic vein thrombosis indicate prothrombotic state from anti-PF4 antibodies.
Can mimic HIT with arterial/venous thrombosis and thrombocytopenia, but lacks the specific temporal correlation with heparin initiation seen here.
Explains high D-dimer and thrombocytopenia, but typically presents with bleeding rather than isolated massive thrombosis and normal fibrinogen/PT/PTT implied by 'other values within normal limits'.

top5.diagnosis: Paradoxical Embolism via Patent Foramen Ovale
top5.rationale: Could explain concurrent venous and arterial clots, but does not account for the profound thrombocytopenia or the specific post-heparin timeline.

top5.diagnosis: Budd-Chiari Syndrome secondary to Hypercoagulable State
top5.rationale: The hepatic vein filling defects are a hallmark of Budd-Chiari, which is likely a manifestation of the underlying systemic hypercoagulability (HIT) rather than an independent primary diagnosis.

top5.diagnosis: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) with Arterial and Venous Thrombosis
top5.rationale: Classic timeline (day 15 post-exposure), severe thrombocytopenia confirmed by citrate tube, and paradoxical multi-territory arterial/venous clots despite anticoagulation.
Must be ruled out as a mimic or co-factor given the combination of arterial stroke, venous PE/DVT, and thrombocytopenia in a patient without traditional vascular risk factors.
Considered if rapid multi-organ involvement (brain, lung, liver veins) progresses; however, the specific drug exposure makes HIT more likely initially.

top5.diagnosis: Paradoxical Embolism via Patent Foramen Ovale (PFO)
top5.rationale: Explains simultaneous venous (PE, DVT, hepatic vein) and arterial (stroke) events, though it does not account for the profound thrombocytopenia.
Hypercoagulability causing migratory thrombophlebitis and strokes can present with thrombocytopenia due to consumption or marrow infiltration, but lacks the temporal link to heparin.
The markedly elevated myoinositol (>13 mM) is a specific MRS biomarker for low-grade glial tumors, distinguishing them from demyelination or ischemia despite the lack of enhancement.

While less likely given the high myoinositol (typically associated with glial origin), PCNSL can present as non-enhancing infiltrative lesions in young adults and must be ruled out via biopsy if MRS interpretation is ambiguous.
The prominent psychiatric/behavioral changes and basal ganglia involvement fit the clinical phenotype, though the specific MRS profile strongly argues against this being the primary etiology.

top5.diagnosis: Mitochondrial Cytopathy (e.g., MELAS or Leigh-like spectrum)
top5.rationale: Basal ganglia predilection and stroke-like episodes are classic, but the absence of lactate peaks on MRS and normal metabolic workup makes this unlikely compared to neoplasm.
Diffusion-weighted imaging was unremarkable, effectively ruling out acute ischemia, and chronic infarcts do not typically produce such extreme elevations in myoinositol.

top5.diagnosis: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) with Arterial and Venous Thrombosis
top5.rationale: Classic timeline (day 15 post-exposure), severe thrombocytopenia, and simultaneous arterial (stroke) and venous (PE, DVT, hepatic vein) thromboses in a patient on enoxaparin without monitoring.
Can mimic HIT with thrombocytopenia and multi-territory arterial/venous clots; must be ruled out as a primary cause or concurrent condition given the lack of typical cardiovascular risk factors.
Consider if there is rapid progression of multiple organ infarctions (brain, lung, liver) within days, though the specific drug exposure makes HIT more likely initially.

top5.diagnosis: Paradoxical Embolism via Patent Foramen Ovale (PFO)
top5.rationale: Explains the stroke in the setting of DVT/PE, but does not account for the severe thrombocytopenia or hepatic vein involvement, making it an incomplete explanation compared to HIT.

top5.diagnosis: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) secondary to occult malignancy
top5.rationale: Post-surgical state and unexplained RUQ pain could suggest underlying cancer triggering DIC, which causes both bleeding/thrombocytopenia and thrombosis, though the specific pattern favors HIT.
Markedly elevated myoinositol is a specific metabolic hallmark of low-grade gliomas due to osmotic regulation in tumor cells, fitting the non-enhancing, infiltrative MRI pattern.
A primary differential for diffuse non-enhancing gliomas with similar spectroscopic profiles, though myoinositol elevation is often more pronounced in astrocytic lineages.
The molecular subtype most associated with this demographic and imaging phenotype; while 2-HG would be the definitive marker, the mI elevation supports the glial nature of the lesion.
Describes the diffuse infiltration across multiple lobes without mass effect or enhancement, which is now classified under diffuse gliomas but represents the specific morphological presentation here.
Considered due to young age and cortical/subcortical involvement, but less likely given the lack of typical 'bubbly' appearance and the significant myoinositol elevation favoring pure glial origin.

top5.diagnosis: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) with Arterial and Venous Thrombosis
top5.rationale: Classic timing (day 15 post-exposure), severe thrombocytopenia, and simultaneous arterial/venous clots fit HIT perfectly; the 'unremarkable' head CT is a red herring as MRI confirmed infarcts.

Explains multi-territory strokes, PE, and DVT in a patient without traditional vascular risk factors, though it does not account for the acute drop in platelets to 43k unless catastrophic APS is present.

top5.diagnosis: Paradoxical Embolism via Patent Foramen Ovale (PFO)
top5.rationale: Links the venous thromboses (DVT/PE) to the arterial strokes, but fails to explain the significant thrombocytopenia or the suprahepatic vein involvement without an underlying hypercoagulable state like HIT.

A strong alternative for unprovoked multi-site thrombosis in a 63-year-old, potentially explaining RUQ pain (metastasis?), but less likely to cause such profound isolated thrombocytopenia without other cytopenias.

top5.diagnosis: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) secondary to Sepsis
top5.rationale: Fever and high D-dimer suggest DIC, but normal fibrinogen/PT/PTT (implied by 'other values within normal limits') and the specific pattern of large vessel thrombosis rather than microvascular bleeding make this less likely than HIT.

top5.diagnosis: Diffuse Low-Grade Glioma (e.g., Oligodendroglioma or Astrocytoma)
top5.rationale: The markedly elevated myoinositol on MRS is a specific metabolic signature for low-grade gliomas, explaining the non-enhancing infiltrative lesion and focal deficits despite negative biopsy/cytology.

Can present as diffuse T2 hyperintensity with restricted diffusion absent in early stages; however, the lack of enhancement and normal CSF make this less likely than glioma, but it remains a critical mimic to exclude.

Explains the psychiatric/behavioral changes and basal ganglia involvement, but typically shows different MRS patterns (normal/high NAA) and would likely have positive antibodies or inflammatory markers in CSF.

top5.diagnosis: Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy (e.g., MELAS or Leigh Syndrome variant)
top5.rationale: Basal ganglia lesions and stroke-like episodes fit, but the absence of lactate peak on MRS and normal angiography/metabolic workup strongly argues against this.

top5.diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
top5.rationale: A diagnosis stated in history that might be considered if organic findings are deemed incidental, but the objective neurologic signs (hemiparesis, hypesthesia) and structural MRI abnormalities rule out pure psychiatric etiology.

The markedly elevated myoinositol (>13 mM) is a specific metabolic signature for low-grade gliomas, particularly astrocytomas, distinguishing them from demyelination or ischemia despite the lack of enhancement.

While less common than astrocytoma in this age group without calcification mentioned, oligodendrogliomas also present as non-enhancing T2 hyperintense lesions with elevated choline and can show high myoinositol, fitting the indolent clinical course.

Unilateral hemispheric atrophy with progressive deficits fits the imaging pattern, but the extreme myoinositol elevation is atypical for pure inflammatory processes, making this a lower-probability mimic.

Basal ganglia/insular involvement suggests vascular territory, but normal DWI/PWI and the chronicity (4 weeks) plus specific MRS profile (high mI, not just lactate/lipids) argue strongly against simple ischemia.

Typically enhances, but rare indolent forms or steroid-modified presentations might appear non-enhancing; however, the MRS profile usually shows higher lipid peaks and different choline ratios than seen here.

The normal barium swallow, normal endoscopy with biopsies, and normal labs effectively rule out organic obstruction or inflammation, leaving functional disorder as the diagnosis of exclusion that fits the persistent globus and anxiety-driven avoidance.

top5.diagnosis: Esophageal Eosinophilic Esophagitis (EoE) missed on initial biopsy
top5.rationale: While biopsies were reported normal, EoE can be patchy; however, given the explicit statement of normal biopsies, this is less likely than functional causes unless sampling error occurred, but remains a critical organic mimic to consider if symptoms persist despite psychological treatment.

top5.diagnosis: Globus Pharyngeus secondary to Anxiety/Depression relapse
top5.rationale: The patient's history of self-harm and current anxiety about solids lodging suggests a psychogenic origin where the sensation of a lump drives the behavioral restriction of diet, mimicking dysphagia without true mechanical blockage.

Although barium swallow was normal, early achalasia can present with intermittent dysphagia and normal initial imaging; the prolonged water swallowing time hints at motility issues, though the lack of regurgitation or weight loss makes this less probable.

This is a rare cause of postprandial discomfort in adolescents, but typically presents with vomiting and significant weight loss, which are absent here, making it a low-probability outlier included for completeness of structural differentials.

top5.diagnosis: Ovarian steroid cell tumor (lipid cell type)
top5.rationale: Unifies severe hyperandrogenism with normal DHEAS and a solid ovarian mass, explaining the virilization without adrenal pathology.
A primary differential for an androgen-secreting ovarian neoplasm in a young woman, though less likely given the specific imaging characteristics of a lipid-rich lesion.

top5.diagnosis: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) with concurrent ovarian cystadenoma
top5.rationale: Explains metabolic features (acanthosis, obesity) but fails to account for testosterone levels >1000 ng/dL or clitoromegaly, making it an incomplete unifying diagnosis.

top5.diagnosis: Adrenal carcinoma with ectopic ovarian metastasis
top5.rationale: Highly unlikely due to normal adrenal CT and normal DHEAS, but considered because adrenal tumors are common causes of rapid virilization.

top5.diagnosis: Cushing's syndrome (ectopic ACTH or adrenal source)
top5.rationale: Excluded by normal urinary free cortisol and dexamethasone suppression test, despite clinical overlap in weight gain and hypertension.
The markedly elevated myoinositol is a specific MRS marker for low-grade glial tumors, explaining the mass-like signal without enhancement or diffusion restriction better than inflammatory causes.

Can present with T2 hyperintensity and high choline/myoinositol ratios; however, lack of enhancement and normal CSF cytology make this less likely but still a critical 'challenger' diagnosis to exclude via biopsy if imaging remains ambiguous.

Explains the clinical deficits and MRI findings, but typically shows lower myoinositol elevations than seen here and often has some degree of enhancement or different spectroscopic profile in acute phases.

Canavan disease is defined by massive NAA elevation, which contradicts the decreased NAA/creatine ratio here, making this a strong negative predictor that should be explicitly ruled out rather than considered primary.

While the patient has depressive symptoms, the objective structural changes on MRI (atrophy, signal abnormality) and specific metabolic shifts on MRS cannot be explained by a purely psychiatric diagnosis, rendering it an insufficient explanation for the organic findings.

top5.diagnosis: Ovarian steroid cell tumor, not otherwise specified (NOS)
top5.rationale: The hallmark is severe hyperandrogenism (testosterone >1000 ng/dL) with normal DHEAS and a solid ovarian mass; steroid cell tumors are the most common cause of this specific biochemical profile in premenopausal women.

A sex cord-stromal tumor that produces androgens; while often associated with lower testosterone levels than steroid cell tumors, it fits the solid adnexal mass and virilization, though clitoromegaly suggests a more aggressive or higher-output lesion like rank 1.
These rare ovarian tumors produce high levels of testosterone directly from hilar Leydig cells, causing rapid virilization and matching the imaging findings of a small, well-defined solid nodule.

top5.diagnosis: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) with concurrent ovarian neoplasm
top5.rationale: The patient has classic PCOS features (acanthosis nigricans, oligomenorrhea, obesity), but PCOS alone cannot explain testosterone >1000 ng/dL or clitoromegaly; the mass may be an incidental benign cystadenoma or stromal hyperplasia co-occurring with severe hyperandrogenic PCOS.

top5.diagnosis: Adrenal rest tumor of the ovary
top5.rationale: Ectopic adrenal tissue within the ovary can form a steroid-producing tumor mimicking an adrenal adenoma biochemically (high testosterone, normal DHEAS if purely gonadal origin) and radiologically as a solid ovarian mass.
Testosterone >200 ng/dL with normal DHEAS localizes to ovary; solid MRI lesion and absence of striae/myopathy despite Cushingoid features suggest pure androgenic steroid cell tumor.
Classic presentation of severe virilization (clitoromegaly) and high testosterone from a small (<2 cm) unilateral solid ovarian mass in a premenopausal woman.
Common sex cord-stromal tumor causing virilization; typically presents as a solid adnexal mass with suppressed gonadotropins due to negative feedback.
Rare but highly androgenic tumor that fits the profile of extreme testosterone elevation and clitoromegaly with a discrete solid ovarian lesion.

top5.diagnosis: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) with concurrent ovarian neoplasm
top5.rationale: Explains acanthosis nigricans, obesity, and oligomenorrhea, but cannot account for testosterone >1000 ng/dL or clitoromegaly, necessitating a dual diagnosis.

top5.diagnosis: Ovarian steroid cell tumor (not otherwise specified)
top5.rationale: Explains extreme testosterone (>1000 ng/dL) and clitoromegaly with a small solid ovarian mass, whereas Sertoli-Leydig tumors are often larger or have different imaging features.

top5.diagnosis: Hilus cell tumor of the ovary
top5.rationale: A rare pure androgen-secreting tumor that fits the high testosterone/normal DHEAS profile and small solid lesion, frequently overlooked in favor of more common sex-cord stromal tumors.

top5.diagnosis: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) with concurrent exogenous androgen exposure
top5.rationale: Challenges the 'tumor' hypothesis by suggesting the ovarian lesion is an incidental functional cyst or hilus hyperplasia, while attributing virilization to undetected supplements or medications not listed in history.

top5.diagnosis: Adrenal rest tumor of the ovary
top5.rationale: Explains the adrenal-like hormonal profile (high testosterone, normal DHEAS due to lack of adrenal enzyme machinery) and solid ovarian mass, distinguishing it from standard sex-cord stromal tumors.
The most common virilizing ovarian tumor, but less likely given the very small size (1.5 cm) and lack of typical heterogeneous/cystic components on MRI, though still a primary differential.
The initial diagnosis is supported by desmin/myogenin positivity and FOXO1 negativity; the post-treatment vacuolated cells represent a known variant of lipomatous change in RMS, not a separate tumor.
While FISH was negative for rearrangement, rare cases lack detectable fusion but retain alveolar histology; however, the embryonal label fits the spindle cell morphology better.

top5.diagnosis: Malignant Triton Tumor (MPNST with rhabdomyoblastic differentiation)
top5.rationale: A key differential for spindle cell sarcomas with skeletal muscle markers; ruled out here primarily by S-100 negativity in the main tumor mass (though vacuolated cells were S-100+).

top5.diagnosis: Pleomorphic Lipoma/Spindle Cell Lipoma with atypical features
top5.rationale: Suggested by the 'lipoblast-like' vacuoles and S-100 positivity in those cells, but excluded by the strong myogenic marker expression (desmin/myogenin) in the non-vacuolated component and aggressive clinical behavior.
Chemotherapy can induce cytoplasmic vacuolation and lipid accumulation in residual tumor cells, creating a pseudolipomatous appearance that must be distinguished from true adipocytic neoplasia.

The initial diagnosis is supported by desmin/myogenin positivity and age/location; the post-excision vacuolated cells represent a rare but documented variant of rhabdomyoblastic differentiation rather than a separate tumor.

top5.diagnosis: Pleomorphic Lipoma / Spindle Cell Lipoma mimicking sarcoma
top5.rationale: While S-100 positive in vacuoles, the strong desmin positivity and myogenin expression in the solid component rule this out, though it remains a key differential for adipocytic lesions in extremities.

The presence of lipoblast-like cells and S-100 positivity raises concern for liposarcoma, but the lack of FOXO1 rearrangement (ruling out myxoid) and negative keratin/SOX10/HMB45 makes this less likely than RMS.

top5.diagnosis: Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumor (MPNST) with heterologous rhabdomyoblastic differentiation (Triton tumor)
top5.rationale: S-100 positivity in some cells could suggest neural origin, but the diffuse desmin/myogenin positivity and specific embryonal morphology favor primary RMS over Triton tumor.

Can present as a deep soft tissue mass in adolescents with eosinophilic cytoplasm and pseudo-alveolar/vacuolated patterns, but typically lacks desmin/myogenin expression and has distinct ASPSCR1-TFE3 fusion.

The initial diagnosis is supported by desmin/myogenin positivity and FOXO1 negativity, while the post-excision vacuolated cells (adipophilin+/S-100+) represent a rare but documented divergent lipomatous differentiation within RMS, not a separate tumor.

Although age and location favor embryonal, the presence of multinucleated giant cells and heterogeneous spindle morphology in the FNA could mimic pleomorphic RMS, which can also exhibit bizarre cytoplasmic changes resembling vacuolation.

top5.diagnosis: Malignant Triton Tumor (MPNST with rhabdomyoblastic differentiation)
top5.rationale: A critical 'overlooked' candidate; MPNSTs are S-100 positive (often focal) and can show heterologous rhabdomyoblastic elements (desmin+), potentially explaining the mixed immunophenotype if the primary neural component was missed or obscured by chemotherapy effects.

ASPS features large polygonal cells with eosinophilic granular/vacuolated cytoplasm and PAS-negative diastase-resistant crystals; however, it is typically Desmin/Myogenin negative, making this less likely unless there is aberrant marker expression or collision tumor.

Vincristine/Irinotecan therapy can induce significant cellular degeneration, vacuolization, and histiocytic reaction (hemosiderin, low mitoses), creating a 'pseudolipomatous' appearance that might be misinterpreted as true adipocytic differentiation or a secondary sarcoma.

The 'embryonal' diagnosis is contradicted by the patient's age (16y), large deep-seated mass, and lack of FOXO1 rearrangement; pleomorphic RMS fits the spindle/ovoid morphology and desmin+/myogenin+ profile better than embryonal.

Strongly suggested by the prominent cytoplasmic vacuolation resembling lipoblasts/adipocytes, PAS-negative diastase-resistant granules/vacuoles, and low mitotic activity, which are classic for ASPS but often misinterpreted as rhabdomyoblastic differentiation.

Desmin positivity supports smooth muscle origin; epithelioid variants can mimic rhabdomyosarcoma morphologically, and the absence of myogenin in the vacuolated subset argues against true skeletal muscle differentiation in those cells.

top5.diagnosis: Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumor (MPNST) with Heterologous Differentiation
top5.rationale: Deep soft tissue mass in a young adult; while S-100 was negative on FNA, MPNSTs can be S-100 negative or focal, and heterologous rhabdomyoblastic differentiation (Triton tumor) explains the desmin/myogenin positivity.

The presence of adipophilin/Oil Red O positive vacuolated cells suggests genuine lipogenic differentiation, contradicting the initial 'no lipogenic differentiation' finding; dedifferentiated components can express desmin.

top5.diagnosis: Ovarian steroid cell tumor (not otherwise specified)
top5.rationale: Extremely high testosterone (>1000 ng/dL) with normal DHEAS and a solid ovarian mass is pathognomonic for this rare sex cord-stromal tumor; the polycythemia is a paraneoplastic effect of erythropoietin secretion.
A specific subtype of steroid cell tumor arising from hilar Leydig-like cells, presenting identically with virilization and an ovarian mass, though often smaller and more benign than NOS variants.

The most common virilizing ovarian neoplasm in young women; while typically associated with lower testosterone levels than seen here, it remains a top differential for any solid ovarian mass causing rapid-onset hirsutism.

top5.diagnosis: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) with concurrent ovarian pathology
top5.rationale: Patient has classic metabolic features (obesity, acanthosis nigricans, hypertension), but PCOS alone cannot explain testosterone >1000 ng/dL or clitoromegaly; likely a comorbid background condition masking the tumor's onset.

top5.diagnosis: Adrenal carcinoma with ectopic ovarian metastasis
top5.rationale: Unlikely given normal adrenal CT and normal DHEAS, but must be considered in any case of severe hyperandrogenism; the 'ovarian lesion' could theoretically represent a metastatic deposit if primary imaging was misleading.

Classic presentation of a brainstem syndrome (one-and-a-half syndrome plus LMN facial palsy) with dissemination in space (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial lesions) and time (enhancing open-ring lesion indicating active demyelination).
Must be considered in Asian patients with severe brainstem syndromes; however, the specific 'open ring' sign and classic periventricular distribution strongly favor MS over NMOSD.
Can present with brainstem encephalitis and multifocal white matter lesions in young adults, but lesions are typically larger, fluffier, and lack the characteristic open-ring enhancement seen here.

Possible given age and multifocal lesions, but ADEM is typically monophasic, associated with encephalopathy (this patient is alert/oriented), and lacks the chronicity markers like distinct open-ring enhancement.
Unlikely due to patient's young age, lack of restricted diffusion on MRI, and the presence of an open-ring enhancing lesion which is pathognomonic for demyelination rather than malignancy.

Classic one-and-a-half syndrome from a left pontine tegmentum lesion combined with dissemination in space (periventricular/juxtacortical/infratentorial) and time (enhancing open-ring lesion), fitting McDonald criteria.
Asian ethnicity increases risk; brainstem syndromes are common, though the specific 'open ring' sign and classic periventricular distribution favor MS over AQP4-IgG positive disease.
Can present with multifocal CNS demyelination including brainstem lesions; often lacks the specific oligoclonal band profile of MS but shares radiologic overlap.
Multifocal white matter lesions fit, but ADEM is typically monophasic, encephalopathic (this patient is alert/oriented), and more common in children, making it less likely than MS.

top5.diagnosis: Primary Angiitis of the Central Nervous System (PACNS)
top5.rationale: A vascular mimic that can produce multifocal ischemic or inflammatory lesions and cranial neuropathies, though the lack of restricted diffusion and presence of an open-ring enhancing lesion strongly argue against this.
Dissemination in space (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial lesions) and time (enhancing vs. non-enhancing), with classic open-ring sign and one-and-a-half syndrome.
Must be excluded in Asian patients with brainstem syndromes; though typical optic neuritis is absent, area postrema or extensive brainstem involvement can mimic MS.
Can present with brainstem encephalitis and facial palsy; often has large, fluffy lesions that may enhance, requiring specific serology to distinguish from MS.

Consider if monophasic presentation with multifocal white matter lesions, though less likely given the distinct open-ring enhancement pattern typical of demyelinating plaques rather than ADEM's ill-defined lesions.
Rare in this demographic but must be considered for enhancing periventricular lesions; however, lack of restricted diffusion and young age make it significantly less likely than inflammatory causes.

Asian ethnicity and severe brainstem syndrome with multifocal lesions are classic for NMOSD, which is frequently misdiagnosed as MS; the open-ring sign can occur in both but AQP4-IgG status is the critical discriminator often overlooked.

Presents with large, fluffy, or ring-enhancing lesions and brainstem involvement including facial palsy/gaze palsies; MOGAD is a distinct entity from MS that requires specific antibody testing and has different treatment implications.

Can present with multifocal enhancing lesions and cranial neuropathies in young adults; while rare, it mimics demyelination on MRI and must be ruled out before steroid administration which would obscure diagnosis.

Frequently causes combined cranial nerve deficits (VII and VI) and multifocal white matter lesions; the 'open ring' sign is less typical but not exclusive to demyelination, and systemic workup is often incomplete in initial presentations.

Monophasic demyelinating disease common in younger patients with multifocal brainstem and supratentorial lesions; though more common in children, adult cases exist and can mimic MS clinically and radiologically.
The systemic arterial supply from the aorta is pathognomonic and explains the recurrent infections and consolidation better than TB alone.
Cystic masses with air-fluid levels are classic for CPAM; sequestration and CPAM often coexist or mimic each other in imaging.
